questions.stem: What number comes next?  7, 12, 17, 22, …

guide.explanation: Each term increases by 5: 7 + 5 = 12, 12 + 5 = 17, and 17 + 5 = 22. Add 5 again to get 27.
guide.shortcut: Check the gaps between consecutive terms. If they stay the same, add that gap once more.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  2, 5, 9, 14, 20, …

guide.explanation: The differences are 3, 4, 5, and 6. The next difference is 7, so 20 + 7 = 27.
guide.shortcut: If the gaps change, write the gaps as a second sequence. Here they increase by 1.

questions.stem: Which pair continues the sequence?  9, 27, 26, 78, 77, …

guide.explanation: The steps alternate ×3 and −1. After 77, multiply by 3 to get 231, then subtract 1 to get 230.
guide.shortcut: Check both requested terms; a pair can start correctly and still finish incorrectly.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  160, 80, 40, 20, …

guide.explanation: Each term is half the previous term: 160 → 80 → 40 → 20. Half of 20 is 10.
guide.shortcut: Check whether each term is multiplied or divided by the same number.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  53, 46, 39, 32, …

guide.explanation: Each term decreases by 7. Subtract 7 from 32 to get 25.
guide.shortcut: Test subtraction when a sequence decreases steadily.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  1.2, 1.6, 2.0, 2.4, …

guide.explanation: Each term increases by 0.4. The next term is 2.4 + 0.4 = 2.8.
guide.shortcut: Think in tenths: 12, 16, 20, 24, then 28 tenths.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  4, 6, 10, 16, 24, …

guide.explanation: The increases are 2, 4, 6, and 8. The next increase is 10, giving 34.
guide.shortcut: Write the differences before trying a complicated rule.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  60, 49, 39, 30, 22, …

guide.explanation: The amounts subtracted are 11, 10, 9, and 8. Subtract 7 next: 22 − 7 = 15.
guide.shortcut: A decreasing sequence can have shrinking gaps.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  8, 11, 16, 19, 24, …

guide.explanation: The changes alternate between +3 and +5. After +5, use +3 to get 27.
guide.shortcut: Check whether the differences repeat in pairs.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  2, 20, 5, 18, 8, 16, …

guide.explanation: The odd-position terms are 2, 5, 8, increasing by 3. The next term is in that group, so it is 11. The even-position terms decrease by 2.
guide.shortcut: Separate the odd and even positions into two smaller sequences.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  1/4, 3/4, 5/4, 7/4, …

guide.explanation: The numerator increases by 2 while the denominator stays 4. The next term is 9/4.
guide.shortcut: With equal denominators, look at the numerators first.

questions.stem: What number fills the blank?  14, 23, __, 41, 50

guide.explanation: The sequence adds 9 each time: 14, 23, 32, 41, 50.
guide.shortcut: Check your missing term against both neighbors.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  5, 8, 13, 20, 29, …

guide.explanation: The gaps are 3, 5, 7, and 9. The next odd-number gap is 11, so the next term is 40.
guide.shortcut: Consecutive odd gaps often appear in square-like sequences.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  50, 48, 44, 38, 30, …

guide.explanation: Subtract 2, then 4, then 6, then 8. Subtract 10 next to get 20.
guide.shortcut: Keep the direction of the change: the gaps grow, but the terms fall.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  12, 19, 15, 22, 18, …

guide.explanation: The rule alternates +7 and −4. The last step was −4, so add 7 next: 25.
guide.shortcut: Label each step with its sign to spot an alternating rule.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  2, 3, 5, 8, 13, …

guide.explanation: Starting with the third term, each term is the sum of the two before it. Thus 8 + 13 = 21.
guide.shortcut: If one-step differences do not fit, try adding neighboring terms.

questions.stem: What number fills the blank?  3, 7, 11, 18, 25, __, 45

guide.explanation: The differences come in pairs: +4, +4, then +7, +7, then +10, +10. The missing value is 25 + 10 = 35; 35 + 10 = 45.
guide.shortcut: Use the term after a blank to check your proposed rule.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  3, 12, 20, 27, 33, …

guide.explanation: The increases are 9, 8, 7, and 6. Add 5 next to get 38.
guide.shortcut: A growing sequence can have shrinking positive gaps.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  −11, −6, −1, 4, …

guide.explanation: The sequence adds 5 each time, even as it crosses zero. The next term is 9.
guide.shortcut: Treat crossing zero like any other addition step.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  4, 6, 9, 13, 15, 18, …

guide.explanation: The increases repeat +2, +3, +4. After +2 and +3, add 4 to get 22.
guide.shortcut: Not every repeating pattern has only two steps.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  2, 6, 18, 54, …

guide.explanation: Each term is multiplied by 3. Thus 54 × 3 = 162.
guide.shortcut: Check ratios when numbers grow much faster than constant addition.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  405, 135, 45, 15, …

guide.explanation: Each term is divided by 3. The next term is 15 ÷ 3 = 5.
guide.shortcut: Verify the same divisor works for every neighboring pair.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  2, 5, 11, 23, …

guide.explanation: Each term is doubled, then increased by 1. So 23 × 2 + 1 = 47.
guide.shortcut: Try a small adjustment after multiplying when simple doubling nearly works.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  4, 11, 32, 95, …

guide.explanation: Each term is multiplied by 3, then reduced by 1. The next term is 285 − 1 = 284.
guide.shortcut: Check the multiply-and-adjust rule on more than one pair.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  6, 3, 1.5, 0.75, …

guide.explanation: Each term is half the previous one. Half of 0.75 is 0.375.
guide.shortcut: Halving 75 hundredths gives 375 thousandths.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  1, 2, 6, 12, 36, …

guide.explanation: The multipliers alternate ×2, ×3. After ×3, multiply by 2 to get 72.
guide.shortcut: Write the ratio above each gap to reveal a repeating pair.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  1, 2, 6, 24, 120, …

guide.explanation: The multipliers are 2, 3, 4, and 5. Multiply by 6 next: 720.
guide.shortcut: The multiplier itself can form a counting sequence.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  0.07, 0.7, 7, 70, …

guide.explanation: Each term is multiplied by 10. Thus 70 becomes 700.
guide.shortcut: Keep track of place value when multiplying by 10.

questions.stem: What number fills the blank?  7, 28, __, 448

guide.explanation: The multiplier is 4. The missing term is 28 × 4 = 112, and 112 × 4 = 448.
guide.shortcut: Check the multiplier on both sides of the blank.

questions.stem: Which pair continues the sequence?  96, 5, 48, 7, 24, 9, …

guide.explanation: The odd-position terms halve: 96, 48, 24, 12. The even-position terms increase by 2: 5, 7, 9, 11. The next pair is 12, 11.
guide.shortcut: Separate odd and even positions before trying a rule for every adjacent pair.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  8, 12, 18, 27, …

guide.explanation: Each term is multiplied by 1.5. Add half of 27 to itself: 27 + 13.5 = 40.5.
guide.shortcut: Multiplying by 1.5 means adding half the number.

questions.stem: What term comes next?  M1, K4, I9, …

guide.explanation: The letters move backward two places: M, K, I, G. The numbers are consecutive squares: 1, 4, 9, 16. Combine the next letter and number to get G16.
guide.shortcut: Check the letter and number rules separately before joining them.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  2, 9, 28, 65, 126, …

guide.explanation: The terms are one more than consecutive cubes: 1³ + 1, 2³ + 1, 3³ + 1, 4³ + 1, and 5³ + 1. The next is 6³ + 1 = 217.
guide.shortcut: Check familiar powers when simple differences and ratios do not fit.

questions.stem: What number comes next?  2, 3, 4, 9, 8, 27, …

guide.explanation: Odd-position terms double: 2, 4, 8, then 16. Even-position terms triple: 3, 9, 27.
guide.shortcut: Read every other term when a single multiplier does not fit.

questions.stem: What is 25% of 84?

guide.explanation: 25% is one quarter. Divide 84 by 4 to get 21.
guide.shortcut: For 25%, halve the number twice: 84 → 42 → 21.

questions.stem: A number is doubled, then 9 is added. The result is 35. What was the original number?

guide.explanation: Undo the last operation first: 35 − 9 = 26. Then undo doubling: 26 ÷ 2 = 13. Check: 13 × 2 + 9 = 35.
guide.shortcut: Work backward with inverse operations, in reverse order.

questions.stem: What is 10% of 350?

guide.explanation: Ten percent is one tenth. Dividing 350 by 10 gives 35.
guide.shortcut: Move the decimal one place left to find 10%.

questions.stem: What is 15% of 80?

guide.explanation: Ten percent of 80 is 8 and 5% is 4. Add them to get 12.
guide.shortcut: Split 15% into 10% plus 5%.

questions.stem: 18 is 30% of what number?

guide.explanation: If 30% is 18, then 10% is 6 and 100% is 60.
guide.shortcut: Scale down to 10%, then scale up to 100%.

questions.stem: A book costs $40 before a 20% discount. What is the sale price in dollars?

guide.explanation: Twenty percent of 40 is 8. Subtract the discount: 40 − 8 = 32.
guide.shortcut: The sale price is 80% of the original, not the discount amount.

questions.stem: Red and blue counters are in a ratio of 2:3. There are 35 counters in total. How many are blue?

guide.explanation: There are 5 equal ratio parts. Each part is 35 ÷ 5 = 7 counters, and blue uses 3 parts: 21.
guide.shortcut: Add the ratio parts before dividing the total.

questions.stem: The average of 12, 16, and a third number is 15. What is the third number?

guide.explanation: The three numbers must total 45. Subtract 12 and 16: 45 − 28 = 17.
guide.shortcut: Convert an average into a total before finding a missing value.

questions.stem: What is 7 + 3 × 8?

guide.explanation: Multiply first: 3 × 8 = 24. Then add 7 to get 31.
guide.shortcut: Multiplication comes before addition unless parentheses change the order.

questions.stem: What is 19 × 6?

guide.explanation: Use 20 × 6 = 120, then subtract one group of 6: 114.
guide.shortcut: Round to a convenient number, then compensate.

questions.stem: What is 3/8 of 64?

guide.explanation: One eighth of 64 is 8. Three eighths is 3 × 8 = 24.
guide.shortcut: Divide by the denominator first when it divides evenly.

questions.stem: Five identical notebooks cost $15. How many dollars do eight notebooks cost?

guide.explanation: Each notebook costs 15 ÷ 5 = 3 dollars. Eight cost 8 × 3 = 24 dollars.
guide.shortcut: Find the price of one item before scaling.

questions.stem: Three consecutive whole numbers have a sum of 72. What is the largest?

guide.explanation: Their middle number is 72 ÷ 3 = 24. The numbers are 23, 24, and 25.
guide.shortcut: For three consecutive numbers, the average is the middle one.

questions.stem: What is the remainder when 157 is divided by 6?

guide.explanation: The greatest multiple of 6 not exceeding 157 is 156. Subtract to get a remainder of 1.
guide.shortcut: Use the nearest lower multiple of the divisor.

questions.stem: One number is three times another. Their sum is 52. What is the smaller number?

guide.explanation: The smaller number is one part and the larger is three parts. Four parts total 52, so one part is 13.
guide.shortcut: Translate “three times” into 3 parts plus 1 part.

questions.stem: Two numbers differ by 8 and have a sum of 46. What is the larger number?

guide.explanation: Their average is 23. Each number is 4 away from the average, so the larger is 27.
guide.shortcut: Add half the difference to the average.

questions.stem: A value rises from 40 to 50. What is the percentage increase?

guide.explanation: The increase is 10. Relative to the original 40, that is 10/40 = 1/4 = 25%.
guide.shortcut: Divide by the original value, not the new value.

questions.stem: A tank is 3/4 full. Half of the water is removed. What fraction of the whole tank is still filled?

guide.explanation: Half of the water remains, so take half of 3/4: 3/4 × 1/2 = 3/8.
guide.shortcut: “Half of” means multiply by 1/2, not subtract 1/2 of the whole tank.

questions.stem: A ribbon is 72 cm long. After 1/3 is cut away, the remaining ribbon is divided into 4 equal pieces. How long is each piece, in cm?

guide.explanation: One third of 72 is 24, leaving 48 cm. Divide 48 by 4 to get 12 cm per piece.
guide.shortcut: Find what remains before dividing it into pieces.

questions.stem: A balance starts at 18 points. Each correct answer adds 5 points and each incorrect answer removes 2. After 4 correct and 3 incorrect answers, what is the balance?

guide.explanation: Four correct answers add 20 points; three incorrect answers remove 6. The final balance is 18 + 20 − 6 = 32.
guide.shortcut: Compute gains and losses separately, then combine them.

questions.stem: A $60 item is reduced by 10%, then reduced by another $6. What is its final price in dollars?

guide.explanation: A 10% reduction removes $6, leaving $54. The additional $6 reduction leaves $48.
guide.shortcut: A dollar reduction and a percentage reduction are different operations.

questions.stem: Two quiz scores average 14 points. A third score raises the average of all three to 16. What is the third score?

guide.explanation: The first two scores total 28. All three must total 48, so the third score is 48 − 28 = 20.
guide.shortcut: Convert both averages to totals before subtracting.

questions.stem: A box has 12 red and 20 blue tokens. How many blue tokens must be removed so that red and blue tokens are equally numerous?

guide.explanation: Keep the 12 red tokens and reduce the blue count to 12. Remove 20 − 12 = 8 blue tokens.
guide.shortcut: Only the named group changes; do not split the difference between groups.

questions.stem: After 6 is added to a number, the result is divided by 3 to give 11. What is the original number?

guide.explanation: Before division the value was 11 × 3 = 33. Before adding 6 it was 33 − 6 = 27.
guide.shortcut: Undo the steps in reverse order.

questions.stem: A 2-metre cord is cut into five 30-cm lengths. How many centimetres remain?

guide.explanation: Two metres is 200 cm. Five pieces use 150 cm, leaving 50 cm.
guide.shortcut: Convert to one unit before subtracting.

questions.stem: How much greater is the square of 9 than the square of 7?

guide.explanation: The squares are 81 and 49. Their difference is 32.
guide.shortcut: You can also use (9 − 7)(9 + 7) = 2 × 16.

questions.stem: What fraction must be added to 5/12 to make 3/4?

guide.explanation: Three quarters is 9/12. Subtract 5/12 to get 4/12, which simplifies to 1/3.
guide.shortcut: Use a common denominator before finding the missing part.

questions.stem: A tray holds 8 cups. What is the smallest number of trays needed to hold 35 cups?

guide.explanation: Four trays hold only 32 cups. One more tray is needed for the remaining 3 cups, so 5 trays are required.
guide.shortcut: A partially filled final tray still counts as a whole tray.

questions.stem: A number is increased by 50% and becomes 42. What was the number?

guide.explanation: The new value is 1.5 times the original. Divide 42 by 1.5 to get 28; half of 28 is 14, and 28 + 14 = 42.
guide.shortcut: Treat the result as three half-sized parts; the original is two of those parts.

questions.stem: Six equal groups contain 54 counters altogether. Two groups are removed, then 7 counters are added. How many counters are there now?

guide.explanation: Each group contains 9 counters. Four groups remain, containing 36; adding 7 gives 43.
guide.shortcut: Find one group, then rebuild only the groups that remain.

questions.stem: Three consecutive odd numbers total 87. What is the smallest?

guide.explanation: The middle number is 87 ÷ 3 = 29. Consecutive odd numbers differ by 2, so the smallest is 27.
guide.shortcut: The middle value equals the average for three equally spaced numbers.

questions.stem: A delivery charge is $4 plus $3 for each parcel. The total charge is $25. How many parcels were delivered?

guide.explanation: Remove the fixed $4 charge: 25 − 4 = 21. Divide by $3 per parcel to get 7 parcels.
guide.shortcut: Subtract the fixed amount before dividing by the per-item amount.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = 3/8 of 80; Q = 35% of 80; R = 0.3 × 100.

guide.explanation: P = 30, Q = 28, and R = 30. Therefore P and R are equal and both exceed Q.
guide.shortcut: Find a common quantity before comparing different representations.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = −3 × 4; Q = 5 − 14; R = −2 × 5.

guide.explanation: P = −12, Q = −9, and R = −10. Among negatives, the number closer to zero is greater.
guide.shortcut: Place negative values on a mental number line.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = 4 × (9 − 2); Q = 4 × 9 − 2; R = 4 × 9 − 4 × 2.

guide.explanation: P and R both equal 28 by the distributive property. Q equals 34 because only 2 is subtracted.
guide.shortcut: Distribute a multiplier to every term inside parentheses.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = 11/12; Q = 7/8; R = 5/6.

guide.explanation: Their gaps below 1 are 1/12, 1/8, and 1/6. The smallest gap belongs to the greatest fraction.
guide.shortcut: Compare distances below 1 rather than dividing all three fractions.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = 7 ÷ 20; Q = 0.305; R = 33%.

guide.explanation: P is 0.35, R is 0.33, and Q is 0.305. Thus P > R > Q.
guide.shortcut: Write each value to the same decimal precision.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = 2³; Q = 3²; R = 4².

guide.explanation: P = 8, Q = 9, and R = 16. Their sum P + Q is 17, which is greater than 16.
guide.shortcut: Evaluate the requested relationship, not only the largest single quantity.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = 60% of 45; Q = 40% of 45; R = 9.

guide.explanation: P is 27 and Q is 18. Their difference is 9, equal to R.
guide.shortcut: The difference between 60% and 40% is 20% of the same base.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = 1 ÷ 0.25; Q = 1 ÷ 0.5; R = 1 ÷ 2.

guide.explanation: P = 4, Q = 2, and R = 1/2. Dividing by a smaller positive number gives a larger result.
guide.shortcut: Division by a fraction below 1 increases a positive number.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = the average of 8 and 20; Q = the average of 11 and 17; R = 15.

guide.explanation: Both pairs total 28, so both averages are 14. Each is less than 15.
guide.shortcut: Pairs with the same sum have the same average.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = 3/5 of 50; Q = 3/5 of 45; R = 2/3 of 45.

guide.explanation: P = 30, Q = 27, and R = 30. P and R are equal; both exceed Q.
guide.shortcut: The same fraction of different wholes does not give the same amount.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = 0.8 × 0.6; Q = 0.8 + 0.6; R = 0.8 − 0.6.

guide.shortcut: Multiplying two positive decimals below 1 makes a smaller product.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = 1/2 + 1/3; Q = 3/4; R = 5/6.

guide.explanation: P = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6, equal to R. In twelfths, 5/6 is 10/12 and 3/4 is 9/12.
guide.shortcut: Simplify one expression before comparing it with the others.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = the increase from 50 to 60 as a fraction of 50; Q = the decrease from 60 to 50 as a fraction of 60; R = 1/5.

guide.explanation: P is 10/50 = 1/5. Q is 10/60 = 1/6. Equal changes divided by different starting values give different rates.
guide.shortcut: Always identify the base used in each fraction.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = 12 × 7; Q = 6 × 14; R = 3 × 28.

guide.explanation: Each product is 84. Halving one factor while doubling the other leaves the product unchanged.
guide.shortcut: Use factor compensation instead of multiplying three times.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = the distance from −7 to 0; Q = −7; R = the distance from 3 to −3.

guide.explanation: Distances are nonnegative: P = 7 and R = 6. Q is −7, so P > R > Q.
guide.shortcut: Distance is a length, not a signed coordinate.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = 15²; Q = 14 × 16; R = 13 × 17.

guide.explanation: P = 225, Q = 224, and R = 221. The products decrease as the factors move equally away from 15.
guide.shortcut: Use (a − b)(a + b) = a² − b² to compare efficiently.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = 1/2 of (30 − 12); Q = 1/2 of 30, minus 12; R = 3.

guide.explanation: P = 18/2 = 9. Q = 15 − 12 = 3, equal to R. The parentheses change what is halved.
guide.shortcut: Track which part of the expression the fraction applies to.

questions.stem:
Compare the quantities. Which statement is true?
P = −2/3; Q = −3/4; R = −5/8.

guide.explanation: In twenty-fourths, P = −16/24, Q = −18/24, and R = −15/24. The greatest is the one closest to zero.
guide.shortcut: Use a common denominator, then remember that negative order reverses size intuition.

questions.stem: Each grid is one whole, divided into equal cells. Let P, Q, and R be the fractions shaded in the labeled grids. Which statement is true?

guide.explanation: P = 3/10, Q = 5/12, and R = 2/6 = 1/3. In sixtieths these are 18, 25, and 20, so P < R < Q.
guide.shortcut: Compare fractions of each whole, not raw numbers of shaded cells.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly a synonym for FRUGAL?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly a synonym for CANDID?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly a synonym for VIGILANT?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly a synonym for PLAUSIBLE?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly a synonym for COAX?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly a synonym for SCRUTINIZE?

guide.explanation: To scrutinize is to inspect closely; it need not involve memorizing or summarizing.
guide.shortcut: Decide the word’s meaning before checking whether a synonym or an opposite is requested.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly a synonym for ALLEVIATE?

guide.explanation: Alleviate means make less severe, not necessarily remove, hide, or delay.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly a synonym for REPLENISH?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly a synonym for PROHIBIT?

guide.shortcut: Decide the word’s meaning before checking whether a synonym or an opposite is requested.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly a synonym for NIMBLE?

guide.explanation: Nimble means quick and skillful in movement; haste, restlessness or low weight alone is insufficient.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly a synonym for STURDY?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly a synonym for TRANQUIL?

guide.explanation: Tranquil means calm and peaceful, not necessarily remote, sleepy, or still.
guide.shortcut: Decide the word’s meaning before checking whether a synonym or an opposite is requested.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly a synonym for TENTATIVE?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly a synonym for REPRIEVE?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly a synonym for CONSPICUOUS?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly a synonym for WARY?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly a synonym for VERIFY?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to AUTHENTIC?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to RIGID?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to DURABLE?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to EXPAND?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to CONCEAL?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to OPTIMISTIC?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to BENEVOLENT?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to TRANSPARENT?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to VOLUNTARY?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to ASCEND?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to MITIGATE?

guide.explanation: Mitigate means make less severe; worsen means make more severe. Inaction does not itself name that opposite change.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to DILIGENT?

guide.explanation: Diligent means showing steady care; negligent means failing to take proper care. Fatigue or inexperience does not establish negligence.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to INCLUDE?

guide.explanation: Include means have as a part; exclude means keep out. Separating or dividing can leave things included in a larger set.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to HOSTILE?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to APPROXIMATE?

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to PERILOUS?

guide.explanation: Perilous means dangerous. Familiarity or predictability does not make something safe.

passage.title: The Missing Sound
paragraphs: The first time Nessa heard her recording of the station, she thought she had made a mistake. The arriving train was there, loud enough to rattle the little speaker. The announcement was there too. But the station she knew had vanished. She had been collecting sounds for a school exhibition called Our Town, and this recording might have belonged to any town at all.

On Saturday she returned before the first train. She held the recorder beside the ticket window, where Mr. Vale was lifting the metal shutter. It caught twice, then sprang upward with a clatter. He laughed. “You will not want that in your exhibition.” Nessa did not answer. From the far bench came the tap of a cane, followed by three notes someone was whistling. Outside, a delivery cart crossed the loose paving stones.

She left these sounds at the beginning of her final recording. At the exhibition, a visitor closed his eyes as the shutter rattled. “I used to buy my ticket there,” he said, before a train had made a sound. Nessa moved the label a little closer to the speaker. She no longer wished she had arrived later.

passage.title: The Missing Sound
paragraphs: The first time Nessa heard her recording of the station, she thought she had made a mistake. The arriving train was there, loud enough to rattle the little speaker. The announcement was there too. But the station she knew had vanished. She had been collecting sounds for a school exhibition called Our Town, and this recording might have belonged to any town at all.

On Saturday she returned before the first train. She held the recorder beside the ticket window, where Mr. Vale was lifting the metal shutter. It caught twice, then sprang upward with a clatter. He laughed. “You will not want that in your exhibition.” Nessa did not answer. From the far bench came the tap of a cane, followed by three notes someone was whistling. Outside, a delivery cart crossed the loose paving stones.

She left these sounds at the beginning of her final recording. At the exhibition, a visitor closed his eyes as the shutter rattled. “I used to buy my ticket there,” he said, before a train had made a sound. Nessa moved the label a little closer to the speaker. She no longer wished she had arrived later.

passage.title: A Clock That Counts Water
paragraphs: For a classroom demonstration, a teacher makes a simple timer from a container with a small opening near its bottom. Water flows through the opening into a tray. The class marks the water level on the container after each minute. If the marks were equally far apart, students could use a ruler to add further minute marks without running the timer again. They discover that this shortcut does not work.

The water level falls farther during the first minute than during the fifth. In this setup, water flows out faster when more water stands above the opening. As the level drops, the flow slows. The container has straight sides, so a given change in level represents the same change in volume wherever that change occurs. The unequal spaces between the minute marks therefore reveal a changing flow, not a changing width.

The students can still use their timer. They refill it to the original starting mark and use the marks established by observation. Enlarging the opening would require a new set of marks. So would replacing the straight-sided container with one that narrows at the bottom. Their device measures elapsed time only when its starting conditions and construction match those used to mark it.

One student proposes keeping the upper container filled to a constant level and measuring the water collected below instead. That design would address the falling level, but it would introduce a new practical task: adding water without changing the upper level substantially. The teacher asks the class to build and test the proposal, not to call it an improvement before seeing how it behaves.

passage.title: The Seat Beside the Door
paragraphs: Until the autumn concert, I thought being useful meant being noticed. I played the trumpet, and when a piece offered even four measures of melody, I leaned toward the edge of my chair. My friend Oren played the bass drum. Sometimes he waited through several pages before lifting a beater. I once asked whether he wished he had chosen an instrument with more to do. He looked at his music and said he had plenty to count.

At our final rehearsal, the director asked us to begin halfway through the longest piece. I knew my entrance well enough to play it in my sleep, or so I had told my brother. But from this unfamiliar starting point, the rests before it seemed to multiply. I watched the flutes, then the director, then my own empty measures. Someone behind me turned a page too soon. I came in a measure early, bright and solitary, and stopped so abruptly that the room seemed to keep the unfinished note.

The director corrected the entrance and moved on. During the break I complained to Oren that it was impossible to find my place without hearing the beginning. He laid his part beside mine and pointed to the changes that led toward my entrance: a short line in the clarinets, a pause, then a low phrase in the cellos. He had marked these on his part even though he played nothing there. “I count,” he said, “but I listen too.”

At the concert, my chair stood beside the backstage door. I could hear a hinge complain whenever an usher slipped through. The director lifted her hands. This time I followed the piece through the rests as closely as through my own notes. The clarinets spoke, the cellos answered, and I entered with the other trumpets. A moment later, Oren struck the drum. The sound was brief, exactly where it belonged.

Afterward my brother praised the trumpet melody. I thanked him, but my eyes went toward the rear of the stage, where Oren was covering the drum. I wanted to describe what he had done. “Did you hear—” I began, then hesitated. My brother was already describing another tune. On Monday, I asked Oren if we could look over our new parts together before rehearsal. He pulled out the chair beside him.

passage.title: When a Blank Is Information
paragraphs: A neighborhood archive contains a ledger listing the tools lent by a repair club. Most entries record a borrower’s name, a date, and the returned tool. For one week in April, the return column is blank. An early description of the ledger called this “the week nobody returned anything.” A student preparing a new exhibit wondered whether the blank could support so confident a claim.

She compared the ledger with a box of separate receipts. Several receipts showed tools returned during that week. She also found a note explaining that the club had moved its desk to another room while the floor was repaired. Perhaps the ledger had not been kept at the temporary desk. That explanation fit the evidence, but the note did not say where the ledger had been. The student therefore did not present the explanation as a fact.

Her exhibit label read: “Return entries are missing for this week. Separate receipts show that some tools did come back. The move during floor repairs may explain the gap.” The new label was longer than the old one. It also asked more of the visitor: instead of offering a simple story, it separated an observation, evidence against one interpretation, and a possible explanation.

The student did not conclude that records were useless. The ledger still contained information unavailable elsewhere, and the receipts were incomplete too. Each source helped test claims made from the other. A blank was a reason to investigate the recording process, not an automatic sign that nothing had happened.

passage.title: A Longer Lunch Line?
paragraphs: The student council proposes opening a second lunch counter. Opponents point out that the dining room already has empty seats. But seats and counters solve different problems. A seat helps a student who has food; a counter serves a student still waiting to receive it. Empty seats alone do not show that the serving system works well.

Before buying equipment, the school should measure where students wait. For a week, observers could record the time students join the line, receive food, and find a seat. They should include busy and quiet days. If most delay occurs before students reach the counter, a second serving point may help. If the slowest step is payment and both counters lead to the same cashier, the purchase may merely produce two lines that stop in the same place.

A temporary second serving table would let the school test the idea without making a permanent commitment. The trial should keep staffing and the menu as comparable as possible and record any unavoidable changes. A faster line on pizza day cannot fairly be compared with a slower line on a day when every meal requires several separate choices.

This proposal is not an argument for postponing improvement indefinitely. It is an argument for buying the improvement students actually need. A week spent finding the delay may save a school from years of owning an expensive answer to the wrong question.

passage.title: The Mapmaker’s Margin
paragraphs: Eli had promised a clean map of the island for the visitors arriving on Sunday. He ruled a border around a fresh sheet and copied the shoreline from the old survey. Then he filled the center with roads, houses, and the names of the three hills. The map looked finished until his aunt asked where the spring path began. Eli pointed to a neat line near the orchard. “That is where the survey puts it,” he said.

They walked there after lunch. The line on his paper became a tangle of nettles on the ground. Beyond it, a narrow trail curved around a fallen tree and joined the path farther uphill. His aunt waited while he sketched the turn on the back of an envelope. “Will you erase the old route?” she asked. Eli said yes, then stopped. He could change the line, but he did not know whether the fallen tree would be cleared next week. A visitor coming later might need a different map.

Back at the table he added a date and wrote, “Temporary detour around fallen tree.” The words would not fit inside his carefully ruled border. He could shrink them until they looked like a trail of ants, or move the border. He moved it. Soon the new margin held another note: “Steps near the jetty are slippery after rain.” The sheet was less elegant than it had been that morning.

On Sunday a visitor studied the notes before choosing a walk. She folded the map along a crease Eli had tried to keep out of the lettering and tucked it into her pocket. He nearly offered her an uncreased copy. Instead, he asked whether the spring path had been easy to find. When she returned that afternoon, there was a small pencil correction beside the jetty. The handrail was loose as well. Eli thanked her and reached for the next sheet.

passage.title: Two Ways to Report a Race
paragraphs: Five teams enter a relay and finish at different times. A notice reports only that Team Cedar finishes third. That statement gives Cedar a position but not a finishing time. Cedar could be a fraction of a second behind the winner or several minutes behind. Rank alone cannot reveal the gap.

A second notice lists each team’s time. It allows readers to calculate gaps as well as determine order. Yet times also need context. If next year’s relay uses a longer course, a slower finishing time would not by itself prove that a team performed worse. Comparing performances requires attention to the conditions being compared.

Rank and time therefore answer different questions. A coach asking “Whom did we finish ahead of?” needs the order. A coach asking “How much time separated us from the winner?” needs the times. Neither measure is useless; the mistake is expecting one to provide information it does not contain.

questions.stem: Which unit is most appropriate for the volume of water in a drinking glass?

guide.explanation: Milliliters measure liquid volume on this scale. Square centimeters measure area, kilometers length, and kilograms mass.

questions.stem: A square's side length is doubled. How does its area change?
choices: It increases by two square units.
It becomes four times as large.

guide.explanation: Area is side²; (2s)² = 4s². The increase depends on s, so it is not a fixed two units.
guide.shortcut: Check whether the claim is always true; a single counterexample defeats an always claim.

questions.stem: Which equation correctly converts 0.07 kilometer to meters?
